context.concept_name: Endpoint integration tests using TestClient or async HTTPX as appropriate

coverage.learning_objective: Test an endpoint through its HTTP interface: write one integration test with TestClient or compatible async HTTPX setup.

required_facts.statement: Create TestClient(app), send an HTTP request with client.get(...) or another request method, and assert response.status_code and response.json() in a test_ function run by pytest.
Use with TestClient(app) as client when the test must execute application lifespan setup and teardown.
Sending a request through TestClient exercises the application's route and dependency resolution rather than only calling the handler function directly.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Calling a handler directly can miss routing or dependency problems. An endpoint integration test exercises the application's HTTP boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Create TestClient(app), send an HTTP request with client.get(...) or another request method, and assert response.status_code and response.json() in a test_ function run by pytest.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use with TestClient(app) as client when the test must execute application lifespan setup and teardown. Sending a request through TestClient exercises the application's route and dependency resolution rather than only calling the handler function directly.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A concrete test has an expected exchange, not just a call that did not crash. For a hypothetical order retrieval, name the request path and method, expected status, and expected public JSON fields. TestClient sends that request through the assembled application, so route and dependency resolution participate. If application setup matters, the context manager adds lifespan execution to the test boundary. A direct handler invocation may still be useful for another purpose, but it does not establish that the registered endpoint resolves its inputs and produces that HTTP exchange. Explain the boundary each test exercises before interpreting a successful assertion as broader evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a synthetic order-retrieval contract, GET /orders/42 should return status 200 and the JSON body {"id": 42, "quantity": 2}. With app configured for that contract, this test demonstrates both assertions:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

def test_get_order():
    with TestClient(app) as client:
        response = client.get("/orders/42")
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert response.json() == {"id": 42, "quantity": 2}
```

Run the test_ function with pytest. The request goes through route and dependency resolution, unlike a direct handler call. The TestClient context executes lifespan setup and teardown when the case requires application-lifetime resources. The status assertion checks the intended HTTP outcome; the JSON assertion checks the expected public content. Neither assertion substitutes for the other.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A direct function call is not an HTTP endpoint test. Execute lifespan with the TestClient context when the case needs it.

video_need.reason: Running controlled success and failure cases makes the observable application boundary and assertions concrete. Focus: Test an endpoint through its HTTP interface: write one integration test with TestClient or compatible async HTTPX setup.

context.concept_name: Required, optional and default input semantics

coverage.learning_objective: Define required, nullable and default inputs: test omitted, null and concrete values for one input.

required_facts.statement: Requiredness depends on whether a declaration supplies a default, while nullability depends on whether its type admits None.
A nullable field without a default still requires presence; writing field: Type | None = None permits both omission and an explicit null.
Test absence, an explicit JSON null and a concrete value as separate requests and compare them with the field's declared default and nullable type.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order note can be required to appear while allowing null as its value. Presence and nullability should not collapse into one "optional" case.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Requiredness depends on whether a declaration supplies a default, while nullability depends on whether its type admits None.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A nullable field without a default still requires presence; writing field: Type | None = None permits both omission and an explicit null. Test absence, an explicit JSON null and a concrete value as separate requests and compare them with the field's declared default and nullable type.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A small presence table can have rows for missing, explicit null and concrete string. With a nullable field lacking a default, missing is not accepted as omission, while null is an admitted value. With a nullable field defaulting to None, both missing and null are allowed. The concrete string is checked against the declared type in either form. This comparison avoids overloading "optional" to mean several different things. Requiredness comes from whether the declaration supplies a default, and nullability comes from the admitted type. Keep both visible when reading or changing the contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare note: str | None without a default with note: str | None = None. The first requires presence but admits null. The second permits omission and explicit null. Send three bodies: one omitting note, one supplying null and one supplying a concrete note. Compare each with the declaration rather than treating them as interchangeable. For a field without a default, missing presence is the issue; for a nullable type, null is a permitted value. A two-axis table labeled presence and value keeps a default from being mistaken for a type choice. This clarifies the input contract before later partial-update behavior uses presence to express intent.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Nullable does not automatically mean omittable. A nullable field without a default still requires presence.

context.concept_name: Trusted host validation

coverage.learning_objective: Enforce accepted HTTP hosts: configure one deployment host allowlist.

teaching_blocks.content: A deployment should accept only intended request host identities. TrustedHostMiddleware checks this Host boundary independently of other metadata.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: TrustedHostMiddleware validates the request Host against an allowed_hosts list and responds with 400 when the host is not allowed.

teaching_blocks.content: Configure app.add_middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=[...]) using domain names; *.example.com permits subdomains and ["*"] permits any host. www_redirect defaults to true and can redirect an allowed non-www host to its www counterpart, so account for it when verifying an allowlist's response.

context.concept_name: Request-scoped async-compatible PostgreSQL session lifecycle

coverage.learning_objective: Own an async-compatible database session for a request: supply and close one async-compatible session per request.

required_facts.statement: AsyncSession maintains mutable state for current database work and is not safe to share across concurrent tasks; use a separate session for each concurrent unit of work.
Build an async_sessionmaker bound to an async engine and use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session for the request's unit of work.
A request dependency can yield a session from its async context, leaving session cleanup to that context on both normal and exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A database session holds mutable state for current work. Concurrent requests should not become concurrent users of one shared session.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: AsyncSession maintains mutable state for current database work and is not safe to share across concurrent tasks; use a separate session for each concurrent unit of work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Build an async_sessionmaker bound to an async engine and use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session for the request's unit of work. A request dependency can yield a session from its async context, leaving session cleanup to that context on both normal and exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the engine-bound factory from the individual session in your ownership sketch. The factory is used to obtain sessions, while an AsyncSession contains mutable state for current database work. Request A and request B should therefore have separate session boxes for concurrent work. Each async context owns closure even when the request fails. Yielding from that context supplies the session to the operation without removing the context cleanup responsibility. This makes the intended request unit of work visible instead of allowing all concurrent users to borrow one mutable object. Session creation and cleanup belong to the same ownership explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Build an async_sessionmaker bound to the async engine. For each request unit of work, use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session. A dependency can yield it from that context, preserving normal and exceptional cleanup. Draw request A with session A and request B with session B. They may share factory setup, but mutable sessions belong to separate concurrent work units. One application-wide session borrowed by both tasks violates this boundary. Follow ownership from creation through dependency use to context exit; cleanup should not depend solely on the successful return branch.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A shared factory is not permission to share one AsyncSession across concurrent tasks.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Own an async-compatible database session for a request: supply and close one async-compatible session per request.

context.concept_name: Graceful termination and shutdown verification

coverage.learning_objective: Verify graceful shutdown: verify termination during one request.

required_facts.statement: Graceful server termination stops old processes accepting new connections and permits active responses and background tasks to finish within configured time limits.
Configure --timeout-graceful-shutdown seconds as the maximum wait before Uvicorn starts terminating remaining requests.
Verify termination during an active request by observing whether its response completes within the limit and whether lifespan cleanup releases the application's shared resources.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A deployment terminates while an order request is active. Graceful shutdown is a bounded opportunity for work and cleanup, not indefinite waiting.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Graceful server termination stops old processes accepting new connections and permits active responses and background tasks to finish within configured time limits.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Configure --timeout-graceful-shutdown seconds as the maximum wait before Uvicorn starts terminating remaining requests. Verify termination during an active request by observing whether its response completes within the limit and whether lifespan cleanup releases the application's shared resources.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Configure --timeout-graceful-shutdown with the supplied maximum wait. Terminate during a controlled active request and observe whether its response completes within that limit. Inspect whether lifespan cleanup releases shared resources. Old processes stop accepting new connections and active responses and background tasks have configured time to finish; after the maximum wait Uvicorn starts terminating remaining requests.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Graceful does not mean unlimited time or guaranteed completion. Verify response behavior and resource cleanup against the bound.

context.concept_name: Service health and readiness checks

coverage.learning_objective: Design health probe contracts: specify one service's probes.

required_facts.statement: A failed liveness probe can cause a container restart, whereas a failed readiness probe removes its eligibility to receive service traffic without requiring a restart.
Readiness can depend on temporary conditions such as required backend availability, even while the process is alive.
Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold that match the service's intended restart and traffic-eligibility contracts.
An HTTP probe regards response status codes from 200 through 399 as success; other codes are failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A process can be alive while unable to serve traffic because a required backend is temporarily unavailable. Liveness and readiness express different decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A failed liveness probe can cause a container restart, whereas a failed readiness probe removes its eligibility to receive service traffic without requiring a restart.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Readiness can depend on temporary conditions such as required backend availability, even while the process is alive. Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold that match the service's intended restart and traffic-eligibility contracts. An HTTP probe regards response status codes from 200 through 399 as success; other codes are failure.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with supplied path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold. Trace a backend outage while the process remains alive: readiness can remove traffic eligibility without requiring restart. Failed liveness can cause restart. HTTP probes classify 200 through 399 as success, other codes as failure. Compare this with the intended probe contract; calling a body "unready" is not enough if its status still counts as successful. Draw restart and traffic eligibility separately so a dependency outage is not automatically treated as proof that restarting is intended.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Alive does not necessarily mean ready. HTTP probe success includes 3xx, not just 200.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Design health probe contracts: specify one service's probes.

practice_anchor.objective: Specify separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks for one service using supplied endpoint paths, port, check periods and failure thresholds. Keep temporary required-backend unavailability in the readiness contract rather than treating it as a reason to restart an otherwise live process.
practice_anchor.success: Both probe mappings contain the intended HTTP path and port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold. The liveness contract permits restart after its failure threshold; the readiness contract removes traffic eligibility after its failure threshold without requiring restart. Endpoint response contracts classify 200 through 399 as success and other codes as failure.

The accompanying contract keeps liveness successful during temporary backend unavailability while readiness returns a failure status, and correctly identifies which probe failure can restart the container and which removes traffic eligibility.

Include a temporary required-backend outage with the process still alive to make the readiness-only effect visible.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Probe contracts distinguish survival from traffic eligibility.
Stay within the current objective: Design health probe contracts. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

context.concept_name: Meaningful contract examples and operation metadata

coverage.learning_objective: Make operation documentation actionable: add realistic examples and operation metadata to one route.

required_facts.statement: Set model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [...]}) on a model to provide schema examples, or use Field(examples=[...]) for field-level examples.
Supply Body(openapi_examples={...}) for named request-body examples in the operation documentation.
Use tags, summary and description on a path operation decorator to describe and group the operation without changing its runtime behavior.
Validate proposed examples with Model.model_validate(example) before including them so their content agrees with the executable model.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Public examples should clarify an order operation's executable contract, not describe incompatible accepted data.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Set model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [...]}) on a model to provide schema examples, or use Field(examples=[...]) for field-level examples.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Supply Body(openapi_examples={...}) for named request-body examples in the operation documentation. Use tags, summary and description on a path operation decorator to describe and group the operation without changing its runtime behavior. Validate proposed examples with Model.model_validate(example) before including them so their content agrees with the executable model.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A documentation example should survive the same model validation a compatible input requires. Pick a synthetic order sample, validate it, and only then include it in schema or named body metadata. If the model has a quantity bound, use a sample satisfying that bound instead of a plausible-looking but invalid quantity. Descriptions and summaries can explain the operation, but they do not loosen the executable constraint. This gives the learner a practical review question: does the example illustrate the declared contract, or does it imply a different one? Publishing a model-valid synthetic sample clarifies the contract without changing runtime behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a synthetic order sample, use quantity 2 with a model whose quantity must be greater than zero. This places the compatible payload in model-level schema examples and validates it before publishing the documentation:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

example = {"quantity": 2}

class OrderInput(BaseModel):
    quantity: int = Field(gt=0)
    model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [example]})

OrderInput.model_validate(example)
```

The sample's quantity satisfies the declared bound; an incompatible sample would mislead about accepted input. For field-level schema examples, use Field(examples=[...]); for named request-body examples, use Body(openapi_examples={...}). Add tags, summary and description to group and explain the operation without assuming they change behavior. The validated synthetic sample illustrates the declared shape rather than a different contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Descriptions do not change runtime behavior. Published examples should validate against their model.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Make operation documentation actionable: add realistic examples and operation metadata to one route.

practice_anchor.objective: Add a realistic synthetic quantity example and operation metadata to one existing order route. Validate the sample, add model-level or field-level schema examples, and configure a named request-body example plus tags, summary and description without changing the handler's behavior.
practice_anchor.success: The quantity-2 sample passes OrderInput.model_validate. Schema metadata and the named body example use that validated sample. The route's tags, summary and description accurately describe its existing behavior, and its handler and quantity constraint remain unchanged.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Documentation metadata clarifies the executable contract rather than implying another one.
Stay within the current objective: Make operation documentation actionable. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

context.concept_name: Test dependency replacement

coverage.learning_objective: Replace dependencies for isolated tests: override and restore one provider in an endpoint test.

required_facts.statement: app.dependency_overrides maps an original provider callable to a replacement callable that FastAPI uses when resolving that dependency in a test.
Assign app.dependency_overrides[original] = replacement, send the test request and assert the replacement's observable behavior.
Restore overrides after the test, such as by resetting app.dependency_overrides to an empty dictionary when no previous overrides existed, to avoid substitutions leaking into other tests.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An endpoint test needs a controlled provider result. Substitute at the declared dependency boundary and exercise its use through HTTP.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: app.dependency_overrides maps an original provider callable to a replacement callable that FastAPI uses when resolving that dependency in a test.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Assign app.dependency_overrides[original] = replacement, send the test request and assert the replacement's observable behavior. Restore overrides after the test, such as by resetting app.dependency_overrides to an empty dictionary when no previous overrides existed, to avoid substitutions leaking into other tests.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Map the original provider callable to a replacement in app.dependency_overrides. Send the request and assert behavior making the replacement observable, such as its synthetic value in the projected result. The mapping uses callables, not provider names or returned values. Restore the earlier override state afterward; reset to an empty dictionary when no prior overrides existed. Trace setup, request, assertion and restoration. Another test should not silently receive this replacement. Limit the override to the controlled input rather than substituting away behavior the test claims to verify.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Overrides left active can alter later tests. Restore the prior state rather than assuming automatic isolation.

video_need.reason: Running controlled success and failure cases makes the observable application boundary and assertions concrete. Focus: Replace dependencies for isolated tests: override and restore one provider in an endpoint test.

context.concept_name: Header and cookie input binding

coverage.learning_objective: Extract request metadata: declare one endpoint's metadata inputs.

required_facts.statement: Declare a request header with Annotated[Type, Header()] so the value is read from headers rather than interpreted as a query parameter.
Header converts underscores in Python parameter names to hyphens by default, and header names are case-insensitive; use alias or convert_underscores=False to control the name mapping.
Declare Annotated[Type, Cookie()] to bind a cookie by name, using a default when its omission should be accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A handler needs a header and a cookie. Explicit source markers keep these metadata inputs from becoming ordinary query parameters.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a request header with Annotated[Type, Header()] so the value is read from headers rather than interpreted as a query parameter.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Header converts underscores in Python parameter names to hyphens by default, and header names are case-insensitive; use alias or convert_underscores=False to control the name mapping. Declare Annotated[Type, Cookie()] to bind a cookie by name, using a default when its omission should be accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare the inputs using Header and Cookie in Annotated types. A header parameter user_agent maps to user-agent by default because underscores become hyphens, and header names are case-insensitive. Use alias or control underscore conversion when the contract requires another mapping. Give a cookie a default when omission is accepted. Trace actual request names to their declarations instead of inferring the source from a metadata-sounding name. Keep source naming and omission behavior separate so a correctly bound cookie also has the intended requiredness.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A metadata-looking name does not automatically bind a header. The declaration and default underscore conversion matter.

practice_anchor.success: The endpoint uses Annotated with Header() for user_agent and Cookie() for the cookie input. user_agent maps to user-agent regardless of header-name case, and the cookie has a default of None.

required_facts.statement: FastAPI raises RequestValidationError for invalid request data and handles it before normal operation logic receives that input.
Assert the default invalid-input response status of 422 and inspect the JSON detail entries to identify the failed input location and error type.
Invalid request input is distinct from a model-validation failure in response or application code, which indicates a server-side bug rather than a client's invalid request.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Malformed order input should be rejected before normal handler logic. That differs from a validation bug in service-generated output.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI raises RequestValidationError for invalid request data and handles it before normal operation logic receives that input.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Assert the default invalid-input response status of 422 and inspect the JSON detail entries to identify the failed input location and error type. Invalid request input is distinct from a model-validation failure in response or application code, which indicates a server-side bug rather than a client's invalid request.

context.concept_name: Configure established request-metrics instrumentation and verify counts, errors and latency with successful, failing and delayed requests

coverage.learning_objective: Configure and verify request metrics instrumentation: instrument one API with a maintained library and exercise three controlled requests.

required_facts.statement: Maintained request instrumentation records request and response counters and a duration histogram around the application boundary rather than requiring each handler to implement its own metrics.

Install the documented PrometheusMiddleware with app.add_middleware(PrometheusMiddleware, filter_unhandled_paths=True) and expose its metrics view with app.add_route("/metrics/", metrics), importing both from starlette_prometheus.
Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, matched route template and response status; filter unmatched paths so arbitrary requested paths do not generate unlimited metric series.

Verify wiring with controlled successful, expected-error and delayed responses, comparing request and response counter changes and the completed responses' duration observations with those known requests.

Interpret the selected middleware's measurement boundary accurately: its response counter is updated even for a raised exception, but its processing-time histogram is observed only when the inner application returns a response.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A metrics endpoint existing does not prove counters and durations measure intended request events. Compare maintained instrumentation against known requests.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Maintained request instrumentation records request and response counters and a duration histogram around the application boundary rather than requiring each handler to implement its own metrics.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Install the documented PrometheusMiddleware with app.add_middleware(PrometheusMiddleware, filter_unhandled_paths=True) and expose its metrics view with app.add_route("/metrics/", metrics), importing both from starlette_prometheus. Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, matched route template and response status; filter unmatched paths so arbitrary requested paths do not generate unlimited metric series. Verify wiring with controlled successful, expected-error and delayed responses, comparing request and response counter changes and the completed responses' duration observations with those known requests. Interpret the selected middleware's measurement boundary accurately: its response counter is updated even for a raised exception, but its processing-time histogram is observed only when the inner application returns a response.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Install PrometheusMiddleware with filter_unhandled_paths=True and expose the /metrics/ view from starlette_prometheus. Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, route template and status. Send a success, expected-error response and delayed response; compare counter changes and duration observations with those controlled requests. This middleware updates its response counter even for a raised exception, but observes processing time only when the inner application returns a response. Counts and completed-response durations therefore need not cover identical paths. Trace them before interpreting aggregates, and filter unmatched arbitrary paths rather than giving every requested path its own series.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A raised exception updates this middleware's response counter but does not produce its normal processing-time observation.

practice_anchor.success: The API exposes /metrics/, filters unmatched paths and uses bounded nonsensitive labels. Each controlled request increments the relevant request and response counters once. Each response returned through the instrumentation boundary adds one duration observation, and the delayed response's duration reflects its controlled delay. Comparisons isolate the exercised routes from metrics-view traffic.

context.concept_name: Distinct create and partial-update contracts

coverage.learning_objective: Preserve partial-update intent: implement one patch extraction.

required_facts.statement: Pydantic tracks explicitly supplied fields in model_fields_set; model_dump(exclude_unset=True) excludes fields that were not supplied.
Extract a partial update with update = model.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) so defaults for omitted fields do not overwrite stored values.
Explicitly supplied None remains supplied under exclude_unset=True; exclude_none=True separately removes None-valued fields and can erase an intentional null update.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A partial update must distinguish "leave unchanged" from "set to null." Presence carries intent separately from value.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Pydantic tracks explicitly supplied fields in model_fields_set; model_dump(exclude_unset=True) excludes fields that were not supplied.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Extract a partial update with update = model.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) so defaults for omitted fields do not overwrite stored values. Explicitly supplied None remains supplied under exclude_unset=True; exclude_none=True separately removes None-valued fields and can erase an intentional null update.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the extracted update data itself before changing storage. An omitted note should be absent from exclude_unset output. An explicitly supplied None note should remain present. A supplied string should remain with its value. These cases encode three different intents under the update contract. A defaulted model value is not enough evidence to tell omission from explicit supply; model_fields_set and exclude_unset retain that distinction. If exclude_none is added, the null-valued case disappears for a different reason. Read the extraction options as intent rules rather than interchangeable cleanup flags. This is why a small output comparison is essential to explaining selective updates.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Stored order data has a note and quantity. An update supplying only quantity should not overwrite note with a default. Extract supplied fields with model_dump(exclude_unset=True); model_fields_set shows explicit fields. Now supply note as None. It remains in exclude_unset output because the caller supplied it and can represent an intentional null under the contract. Adding exclude_none=True removes it separately and can erase that intent. Compare omission, null and concrete values in extracted updates before applying them. The final value alone does not reveal whether a caller supplied the field.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: exclude_unset and exclude_none answer different questions. Removing None can erase an intentional null update.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Preserve partial-update intent: implement one patch extraction.

Without exclude_unset=True, that default could overwrite existing content; with it, the extracted update contains only the supplied title.

context.concept_name: Backward-compatible REST contract changes

coverage.learning_objective: Evaluate compatibility: review one schema change.

required_facts.statement: Changing an omittable request field into a required field rejects requests that were previously accepted, so a schema review must compare requiredness as well as types.
Tightening a type or field constraint can invalidate previously accepted client input; test representative previously valid inputs against the revised model.

Removing or changing a public response field or operation can change a client's documented expectations; compare the generated paths and response schemas with the previous contract before approving the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A revised order model can look cleaner while breaking previously valid clients. Review compatibility against accepted inputs and public outputs, not just new field names.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Changing an omittable request field into a required field rejects requests that were previously accepted, so a schema review must compare requiredness as well as types.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Tightening a type or field constraint can invalidate previously accepted client input; test representative previously valid inputs against the revised model. Removing or changing a public response field or operation can change a client's documented expectations; compare the generated paths and response schemas with the previous contract before approving the change.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare a previous omittable note field with a revised required one. An old request omitting note now fails. Likewise, a tighter quantity constraint may reject a previously valid quantity. Keep representative old inputs and validate them against the revision. On the output side, compare generated paths and response schemas before approving removed or changed fields or operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A matching type name alone does not prove compatibility. Requiredness, constraints, fields and operations also shape client expectations.

context.concept_name: Retrieve resource

coverage.learning_objective: Retrieve a resource through the ORM: retrieve one resource by identity and test the not-found case.

required_facts.statement: Select mapped entities with await session.scalars(select(Entity).where(condition)) and inspect the resulting entity values rather than treating the result as an unbounded application-wide lookup.
Use await session.get(Entity, identity) for a primary-key lookup; it returns the identified entity or None when no row exists.
Add .limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows, and explicitly handle an empty result or None as absence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A request wants a stored order, but a missing row is a valid lookup outcome to handle explicitly. Selection should match the intended identity or bounded condition.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Select mapped entities with await session.scalars(select(Entity).where(condition)) and inspect the resulting entity values rather than treating the result as an unbounded application-wide lookup.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use await session.get(Entity, identity) for a primary-key lookup; it returns the identified entity or None when no row exists. Add .limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows, and explicitly handle an empty result or None as absence.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the retrieval form from the lookup requirement. If the request names a primary-key identity, get directly represents that lookup and has an explicit None outcome. If the requirement is a condition over several rows, select with where represents that condition and limit represents the intended bound. Inspect the resulting entities or empty result rather than assuming every successfully executed selection contains a match. The missing-row case belongs in the workflow before attribute use. This reasoning keeps retrieval precise: identify what is being selected, how many rows are intended, and what absence means for the next application step.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For an identified order, await session.get(Order, identity) returns the entity or None. Trace both branches before using entity attributes. For a conditional selection, use session.scalars with select(Order).where(condition) and inspect the entity values. Add limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows. Compare one matching order, no matching orders and multiple matches under the bound. A result of None and an empty selection both represent absence in their respective lookup forms; neither should be treated as an existing entity. This exercise connects the lookup shape to the result handling rather than turning a selection into an unbounded application-wide search.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A successful lookup operation does not guarantee a row exists. Handle None or an empty result explicitly.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Retrieve a resource through the ORM: retrieve one resource by identity and test the not-found case.

practice_anchor.objective: Retrieve an Order using await session.get(Order, identity), explicitly handle None before accessing entity attributes, and test the lookup with an existing identity and an absent identity.
practice_anchor.success: The existing identity yields the intended Order entity. The absent identity yields None and follows an explicit absence branch without attribute access.

live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide Order, an active async session, and an async function scaffold accepting session and identity. An external harness supplies identity once for an existing Order and once for an absent Order; no setup or persistence changes are required.
live_code.observable_success: The harness verifies that the existing identity returns its Order and the absent identity returns None. The implementation explicitly checks entity is None before any entity attribute access.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show annotated Order retrieval examples: an awaited primary-key lookup branching on None, and an awaited conditional scalar selection with an explicit limit and empty-result handling.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: A bounded selection maps matching persistent rows to entities; absence is a valid query outcome..
Stay within the current objective: Retrieve a resource through the ORM. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Select the intended resource using a bounded query and distinguish a matching row from absence.

context.concept_name: Transaction commit and rollback boundaries

coverage.learning_objective: Choose transaction boundaries: implement one multi-write operation.

required_facts.statement: Use async with session.begin(): around related writes to commit on successful exit and roll back on exceptional exit.
A commit makes transaction changes durable, while a rollback discards uncommitted changes; multiple related writes belong in one transaction when they must succeed or fail together.
After a flush failure, explicitly roll back before reusing that session; a failed flush leaves its transactional state requiring recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two related order writes must succeed or fail together. A transaction makes that joint boundary explicit rather than letting each write be treated as independently durable.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use async with session.begin(): around related writes to commit on successful exit and roll back on exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A commit makes transaction changes durable, while a rollback discards uncommitted changes; multiple related writes belong in one transaction when they must succeed or fail together. After a flush failure, explicitly roll back before reusing that session; a failed flush leaves its transactional state requiring recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Transaction recovery is observable separately from the original failure. In the two-write example, successful completion of the pair belongs to commit; exceptional exit belongs to rollback. A failed flush requires explicit rollback before session reuse even when application code has already caught the error. Therefore the recovery path should mention both the discarded uncommitted changes and the session state that must be recovered. Reporting only that an error was handled obscures whether either responsibility was met. Group the writes because the requirement ties their success together, and keep that requirement visible in the transaction scope.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Place related writes inside async with session.begin(). Successful exit commits; exceptional exit rolls back. Trace a first write followed by a failing second write: the exceptional transaction outcome should discard uncommitted changes rather than report a completed pair. Compare that with successful exit, which makes the changes durable. If a flush fails, explicitly roll back before reusing the session, because its transactional state requires recovery. Follow both data state and session state in the trace: a caught error message alone does not establish that either boundary has been recovered. The grouping should come from the requirement that the writes succeed or fail together, not merely from their proximity in the source file.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Catching a flush exception does not restore the session to usable transactional state. Roll back before reuse.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Choose transaction boundaries: implement one multi-write operation.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement one transaction boundary around two supplied asynchronous order-write helpers so that the writes succeed or fail together, without implementing their persistence details.
practice_anchor.success: Both helper calls run inside the same session.begin() scope. Successful exit commits the pair; an exception escaping the scope rolls back the uncommitted changes. A supplied standalone flush-failure recovery branch explicitly rolls back before session reuse.

live_code.required_skill: Group related asynchronous writes in one transaction and recover session state after a failed flush.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an async operation with an idle session and two already-implemented order-write helpers. Leave the shared transaction scope unfinished. Separately provide a caught standalone flush-failure branch with a rollback placeholder before session reuse; learners do not implement write helpers or exception handling.
live_code.observable_success: The two supplied order writes share one transaction scope. A successful run makes both durable; a failure in the second helper leaves neither write committed. The standalone flush-failure branch awaits session.rollback() before the supplied session-reuse step.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the two order writes visible inside one transaction boundary, with successful exit leading to durable changes and exceptional exit leading to discarded uncommitted changes. Show a separate failed-flush recovery path requiring explicit rollback before session reuse.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Related writes succeed or fail together.
Stay within the current objective: Choose transaction boundaries. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine commit and rollback effects.
The multi-write objective overlaps later persistence-operation concepts, so practice supplies the write helpers and asks learners to implement only transaction grouping and session recovery.

context.concept_name: Bearer-token extraction into an authentication dependency

coverage.learning_objective: Extract bearer credentials from an API request: declare one bearer extraction dependency and verify absent and malformed credentials.

required_facts.statement: A bearer extraction dependency reads a credential from Authorization: Bearer token; receiving the credential does not itself establish that it is valid.
Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] on a handler input and read its scheme and credentials fields to obtain the supplied bearer credential.
With HTTPBearer's default auto_error=True, absent credentials or a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of supplied to the handler; verify absent and malformed Authorization headers separately.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A protected handler first needs to obtain a presented bearer credential. Extracting it is not the same as verifying that it is valid.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A bearer extraction dependency reads a credential from Authorization: Bearer token; receiving the credential does not itself establish that it is valid.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] on a handler input and read its scheme and credentials fields to obtain the supplied bearer credential. With HTTPBearer's default auto_error=True, absent credentials or a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of supplied to the handler; verify absent and malformed Authorization headers separately.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] and read its scheme and credentials fields. A request with Authorization: Bearer followed by a supplied token presents the credential for later verification. With default auto_error=True, absent credentials and a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of passed to the handler. Exercise absent and malformed Authorization headers separately so the extraction gate is visible. Then consider a presented bearer token: obtaining its text establishes only that extraction found a credential, not that its claims or authority are trustworthy. Keep that distinction in the trace so a handler does not mistake possession of a token-shaped value for completed authentication.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: HTTPBearer extracts a credential; extraction does not verify claims or issue a token. Do not use the extracted text as proof of validity.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Extract bearer credentials from an API request: declare one bearer extraction dependency and verify absent and malformed credentials.

practice_anchor.success: A nonempty Bearer credential reaches the handler with its scheme and credential text available. An absent header, a non-bearer scheme, and a Bearer header without credential text are each rejected before the handler executes. Extraction is not treated as proof of credential validity.

live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a minimal FastAPI application with one handler awaiting its bearer dependency declaration and a TestClient scaffold. Use only Authorization header inputs: a nonempty Bearer credential, no header, a non-bearer scheme, and Bearer without credential text. Keep all credential values synthetic.

Each absent or malformed case receives a failure response rather than the handler's success response. Tests establish extraction behavior only, not credential validity.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Bearer extraction locates credentials; it does not verify their claims or issue tokens..
Stay within the current objective: Extract bearer credentials from an API request. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

context.concept_name: Redis cache-aside selection and population

coverage.learning_objective: Implement cache-aside retrieval: add cache-aside retrieval to one read endpoint.

required_facts.statement: Cache-aside keeps a cache in front of a primary store; the primary store remains the source of truth rather than the cache becoming authoritative storage.
On a read, get the cache key first; on a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it to the caller.
Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy data where repeated reads can reuse a copy and the application's staleness requirements permit that reuse.
Construct the cache key from the identity and parameters of the represented result so requests for different results do not reuse the wrong cached value.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Repeated reads of an order may reuse a cached copy, but the database remains authoritative. Cache-aside separates accelerated reads from source-of-truth storage.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Cache-aside keeps a cache in front of a primary store; the primary store remains the source of truth rather than the cache becoming authoritative storage.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: On a read, get the cache key first; on a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it to the caller. Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy data where repeated reads can reuse a copy and the application's staleness requirements permit that reuse. Construct the cache key from the identity and parameters of the represented result so requests for different results do not reuse the wrong cached value.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace a read for order 42. Check its cache key first. On a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it. A later read may reuse that copy if the staleness requirements permit it. Choose the key from the identity and parameters of the represented result: order 43 or a differently parameterized result must not accidentally reuse order 42's value. Compare a hit and a miss in a two-path diagram, keeping both connected to the same represented result. Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy reuse, not a claim that any data can remain cached indefinitely. The cache is a disposable copy; the primary store is still the authority when deciding what the stored order actually is.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A cache hit does not make the cache authoritative. A key must distinguish results whose identity or parameters differ.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Implement cache-aside retrieval: add cache-aside retrieval to one read endpoint.

media.group_title: Cache-aside: recover a miss and reuse a cached result

segments.label: Trace a Redis cache miss, population, and subsequent hit
segments.summary: The application checks Redis before querying the database. In the profile example, the first request finds no cached result: this is a cache miss. The application retrieves the profile from the database, stores a copy in Redis, and returns the response. A subsequent request finds that copy: this is a cache hit, so the application returns it without another database query. Reusing cached results can reduce database reads and improve response times; the speed claims illustrate the benefit rather than guarantee performance for every workload.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the profile request moves through a miss, database retrieval, cache population, and a later hit. Apply the same sequence to the order example; the speed claims are illustrative, not guarantees.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains the read sequence and repeated-read benefit. It does not establish primary-store authority, staleness eligibility, or result-specific key construction; the text supplies those boundaries.

The cache adapter accepts and returns endpoint-ready order results and returns None for a miss. The primary-store adapter returns an existing order result. Use read-heavy order examples whose permitted staleness allows reuse.
live_code.observable_success: Adapter call records show cache lookup first; a hit returns without a primary-store call, while a miss loads the order, stores that result under the same key, and returns it. Keys differ when order_id or representation differs.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an order read splitting into hit and miss paths after lookup of an identity-and-parameters cache key. The hit returns the cached copy; the miss loads from the authoritative primary store, populates the cache, and returns the result. Mark the cache as a disposable copy.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: The cache is a disposable copy and the database remains authoritative.
Stay within the current objective: Implement cache-aside retrieval. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

context.concept_name: Authoring, reviewing and applying Alembic schema migrations

coverage.learning_objective: Manage Alembic migrations: review one reversible migration.

required_facts.statement: Alembic maintains a migration environment and versioned revision scripts that describe schema changes through upgrade() and downgrade().
Generate a candidate revision with alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description", comparing the database schema with supplied target_metadata.
Autogeneration produces candidate changes that require manual review and correction; it does not reliably infer every schema intent such as table or column renames.
Apply revisions with alembic upgrade head and exercise alembic downgrade revision on a test database to verify a proposed reversal before using it operationally.
Review an autogenerated drop-and-add pair for a possible rename before applying it; dropping a column deletes the data stored in that column, so an apparent reversal may not recover that data.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A schema change needs a reviewed revision, not an assumption that automatic comparison understands every intended change.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Alembic maintains a migration environment and versioned revision scripts that describe schema changes through upgrade() and downgrade().

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Generate a candidate revision with alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description", comparing the database schema with supplied target_metadata. Autogeneration produces candidate changes that require manual review and correction; it does not reliably infer every schema intent such as table or column renames. Apply revisions with alembic upgrade head and exercise alembic downgrade revision on a test database to verify a proposed reversal before using it operationally. Review an autogenerated drop-and-add pair for a possible rename before applying it; dropping a column deletes the data stored in that column, so an apparent reversal may not recover that data.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Generate a candidate with alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description" using target_metadata. Inspect upgrade and downgrade, especially a drop-and-add pair that might actually represent a rename. Dropping a column deletes its data; a later apparent reversal may not recover it. Apply with alembic upgrade head and exercise the proposed downgrade on a test database. Candidate generation, review and reversal verification are separate steps.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Autogeneration is a candidate, not complete schema intent. A downgrade that recreates a column does not necessarily recover deleted data.

Choose a deterministic ordering with a unique tie-breaker when the primary sort value can repeat, so page boundaries do not depend on unspecified ordering among tied rows.
OFFSET skips the requested number of result rows and LIMIT caps the number returned afterward; use the same filter and unique ordering for the page selections.
Bound accepted page size and offset with declared numeric constraints and compute offset from the requested page contract instead of accepting an unbounded read.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders listing should return a bounded window from a defined ordered result. Page boundaries need stable tie-breaking rather than unspecified order among equal sort values.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Build bounded results with select(Entity).where(predicate).order_by(order_columns).limit(page_size).offset(offset).

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a deterministic ordering with a unique tie-breaker when the primary sort value can repeat, so page boundaries do not depend on unspecified ordering among tied rows. OFFSET skips the requested number of result rows and LIMIT caps the number returned afterward; use the same filter and unique ordering for the page selections. Bound accepted page size and offset with declared numeric constraints and compute offset from the requested page contract instead of accepting an unbounded read.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same filter and ordering for page selections, with limit(page_size) and offset(offset). If several orders share the primary sort value, add a unique tie-breaker. In a hypothetical page size of three with offset three, OFFSET skips the first three result rows and LIMIT caps the next returned rows at three. Compare adjacent pages using the same predicate and unique ordering; changing the filter would change the result set being paged. Bound accepted page size and offset with numeric constraints and compute the offset according to the supplied page contract. This is bounded selection over an ordered result, not permission for a client to request an unlimited read.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: LIMIT caps rows after OFFSET skips them. A repeated primary sort value needs a unique tie-breaker for deterministic ordering.

context.concept_name: Injection-resistant database and input handling

coverage.learning_objective: Bind query values safely: parameterize one unsafe query.

required_facts.statement: Parameterized queries keep SQL structure separate from caller-controlled data instead of interpolating that data into executable SQL text.
Use a SQLAlchemy expression such as select(Entity).where(Entity.field == supplied_value) so the supplied value becomes a bound value rather than SQL syntax.
For a supplied textual query, use text("... WHERE field = :value") with an execute parameter dictionary {"value": supplied_value}, not string formatting or concatenation of the input.
Parameters represent data values, not arbitrary table names, column names or sort direction; map a requested structural choice through a defined allowlist when binding a value cannot express it.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A caller-supplied order reference is data, not SQL structure. Keep it bound as a value rather than concatenating it into executable query text.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Parameterized queries keep SQL structure separate from caller-controlled data instead of interpolating that data into executable SQL text.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use a SQLAlchemy expression such as select(Entity).where(Entity.field == supplied_value) so the supplied value becomes a bound value rather than SQL syntax. For a supplied textual query, use text("... WHERE field = :value") with an execute parameter dictionary {"value": supplied_value}, not string formatting or concatenation of the input. Parameters represent data values, not arbitrary table names, column names or sort direction; map a requested structural choice through a defined allowlist when binding a value cannot express it.

Now compare a client-selected sort direction: a parameter cannot stand for arbitrary SQL structure. Map that structural choice through a defined allowlist. Separate value binding from structural selection so a safe mechanism for one is not assumed to solve the other.

context.concept_name: Create resource

coverage.learning_objective: Create a resource through the ORM: insert one mapped resource and verify its stored state.

required_facts.statement: Construct Entity(field=value, ...) with the supplied fields and call session.add(entity) to put a new entity into the pending insert state.
await session.flush() emits the pending insert and assigns database-generated identity values back to the mapped entity when supported by its mapping and database.
Commit the successful creation with await session.commit() or a successfully exiting session.begin() context; a flush alone is not a commit.
Verify the generated identity and committed field values with await fresh_session.get(Entity, identity) in an independent session rather than checking only that a Python object was constructed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A newly constructed order object is not yet evidence of a committed database row. Creation moves through pending insertion, flush and commit.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Construct Entity(field=value, ...) with the supplied fields and call session.add(entity) to put a new entity into the pending insert state.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: await session.flush() emits the pending insert and assigns database-generated identity values back to the mapped entity when supported by its mapping and database. Commit the successful creation with await session.commit() or a successfully exiting session.begin() context; a flush alone is not a commit. Verify the generated identity and committed field values with await fresh_session.get(Entity, identity) in an independent session rather than checking only that a Python object was constructed.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Construct the entity and add it to the session. It is now pending insertion. Flush emits the insert and can assign database-generated identity values back when the mapping and database support it. Commit through the transaction contract to make successful creation durable. Then use an independent session to retrieve that identity and verify committed fields. Trace object construction, pending state, insert and durable lookup separately: an id observed after flush does not make flush a commit. The independent lookup verifies persistence rather than only re-reading the same constructed Python object. This gives the creation operation evidence at the stored-state boundary it claims to change.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Flush is not commit. A constructed object or assigned identity alone does not prove durable creation.

coverage.learning_objective: Delete a resource through the ORM: delete one identified resource and verify its absence.

Commit the successful deletion under the transaction contract and roll back a failed deletion instead of reporting an uncommitted removal as durable.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Load the intended entity with await session.get(Entity, identity) and handle None as absence before attempting deletion.

context.concept_name: JWT signature, issuer, audience and expiry verification

coverage.learning_objective: Verify JWTs before trusting claims: protect one endpoint with token verification.

required_facts.statement: JWT decoding without verification reveals claims but does not establish that the claims are trustworthy.

Verify with jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=[allowed_algorithm], issuer=expected_issuer, audience=expected_audience, options={"require": ["exp", "iss", "aud"]}); choose the allowed algorithm from trusted configuration, not from the token alone.
Expiration and not-before claims constrain token time validity; checks for a claim's value are distinct from requiring that the claim be present.
Treat a library verification exception as an invalid credential and reject the protected request rather than using its unverified claims.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A token can reveal claims when decoded without verification, but those claims remain untrusted. The verifier establishes a configured trust boundary before protected output is allowed.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: JWT decoding without verification reveals claims but does not establish that the claims are trustworthy.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Verify with jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=[allowed_algorithm], issuer=expected_issuer, audience=expected_audience, options={"require": ["exp", "iss", "aud"]}); choose the allowed algorithm from trusted configuration, not from the token alone. Expiration and not-before claims constrain token time validity; checks for a claim's value are distinct from requiring that the claim be present. Treat a library verification exception as an invalid credential and reject the protected request rather than using its unverified claims.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Keep three columns in the token review: readable claim, required claim and verified claim value. Opening a token without verification fills only the first kind of observation. The verifier must use trusted algorithm and key configuration, require the intended claims, and check their values under issuer, audience and time policy. Expiration and not-before constrain validity, but a value check and a presence requirement are not interchangeable. If the library rejects verification, the protected request must reject the credential rather than reuse the readable payload. That final rejection branch is part of the trust boundary, not an optional diagnostic detail.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the allowed algorithm, key, issuer and audience from trusted configuration, not the token alone. Decode with verification and explicitly require exp, iss and aud. Requiring a claim and checking its value are distinct: a time check is not the same as guaranteeing the claim is present. Expiration and not-before constrain time validity. Trace a token through verification, then trusted context; a library verification exception should lead to credential rejection rather than fallback use of unverified claims. Compare a token merely opened for inspection with one accepted under all configured checks. The readable payload in the first case is information, not evidence that the caller is entitled to use its asserted identity or permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Decoding without verification is not authentication. The token itself must not choose the allowed algorithm.

context.concept_name: Freshness policy

coverage.learning_objective: Control cached-data freshness after writes: implement expiry and write invalidation for one cached resource.

required_facts.statement: Choose a cache TTL from the tolerated staleness window: a shorter TTL refreshes sooner but causes more primary-store reads, while a longer TTL reduces reads and can serve older values longer.
For a string cache entry, pass ex=seconds to Redis set(key, value, ex=seconds) to assign an expiry when writing it.
After the primary record changes, delete its cache key so the next cache-aside read reloads it instead of serving the old copy.

Inspect ttl(key): it reports remaining seconds, -1 for a key without expiry and -2 for an absent key; change the primary record and verify that invalidation makes the next read return the changed value.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A cached order can become stale after the primary row changes. Freshness policy combines tolerated lifetime with invalidation of the derived copy.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a cache TTL from the tolerated staleness window: a shorter TTL refreshes sooner but causes more primary-store reads, while a longer TTL reduces reads and can serve older values longer.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: For a string cache entry, pass ex=seconds to Redis set(key, value, ex=seconds) to assign an expiry when writing it. After the primary record changes, delete its cache key so the next cache-aside read reloads it instead of serving the old copy. Inspect ttl(key): it reports remaining seconds, -1 for a key without expiry and -2 for an absent key; change the primary record and verify that invalidation makes the next read return the changed value.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a TTL from the permitted staleness window and set it using Redis set with ex=seconds. A shorter lifetime refreshes sooner but causes more primary reads; a longer one can serve older values longer. Inspect ttl(key): remaining seconds show expiry, -1 means no expiry, and -2 means no key. After changing the primary order, delete the cache key and verify that the next cache-aside read reloads the changed value. Trace the old copy, committed primary change, invalidation and reload. The TTL limits lifetime while invalidation responds to known changes; neither should be described as making the cache the authority. Select synthetic old and new notes so that a returned stale value is easy to distinguish.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A key with ttl -1 has no expiry, not an absent key. Deleting the stale copy makes the next cache-aside read reload it.

media.group_title: Expiry and invalidation keep derived copies fresh

segments.label: How expiry and write invalidation trigger a fresh read
segments.summary: A cached project list becomes stale when a new project is added to the database without changing the cached copy. Giving the cache key a 60-second lifetime allows that old copy to remain until expiry; the next read then misses and reloads from the database. Write invalidation instead deletes the affected key when the primary data changes, so the next read reloads rather than returning the old list. Every relevant write path needs that deletion. Combining expiry with write invalidation limits how long a missed invalidation can leave an old copy available.

context.concept_name: Safe failure policy

coverage.learning_objective: Preserve correctness when the cache is unavailable: implement a correct database fallback for one cache-backed read.

required_facts.statement: Catch Redis connection and timeout exceptions at the cache boundary so the application can apply its declared cache-outage policy rather than letting an incidental cache exception choose the outcome.
When the cache is only an acceleration layer and the primary store is available, the miss path can load and return the primary-store value without a successful cache read or write.
Configure finite socket_connect_timeout and socket_timeout values on the Redis client so a failed cache does not cause unbounded connection or response waits.

Verify the policy with a controlled failing cache dependency, asserting the primary-store result or the declared failure outcome rather than assuming that a cache outage is equivalent to lost primary data.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A cache outage should follow an explicit service policy. When caching is only acceleration, a failed cache does not by itself mean primary data is lost.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Catch Redis connection and timeout exceptions at the cache boundary so the application can apply its declared cache-outage policy rather than letting an incidental cache exception choose the outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: When the cache is only an acceleration layer and the primary store is available, the miss path can load and return the primary-store value without a successful cache read or write. Configure finite socket_connect_timeout and socket_timeout values on the Redis client so a failed cache does not cause unbounded connection or response waits. Verify the policy with a controlled failing cache dependency, asserting the primary-store result or the declared failure outcome rather than assuming that a cache outage is equivalent to lost primary data.

required_facts.statement: Use an authenticated publisher event identifier as the deduplication key and retain the deduplication record across application restarts for the required replay window.

teaching_blocks.content: A webhook event can arrive twice or concurrently. Prevent repeated business effects with durable authenticated event identity, not only a process-local memory check.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use an authenticated publisher event identifier as the deduplication key and retain the deduplication record across application restarts for the required replay window.

Store the identifier atomically with durable state changes in a transaction backed by uniqueness. coverage.learning_objective: Choose bounded safe retries: specify one operation's retry policy.

required_facts.statement: Automatically repeating a non-idempotent request can duplicate effects; retry only when the method or application contract establishes idempotency or proves that the original request was not applied.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary

context.concept_name: Object-level authorization against the authenticated principal

coverage.learning_objective: Enforce object ownership: protect one item endpoint.

required_facts.statement: An endpoint taking an object identifier must check the caller's permission for that specific object; a valid identifier and authenticated caller do not establish ownership.
Enforce the object boundary by selecting with both object identity and the authorized owner or tenant context, rather than trusting an owner identifier from caller-controlled input.
Create distinct authorized contexts and verify that each can access its permitted object but cannot obtain or change the other context's object by substituting its identifier.

teaching_blocks.content: An authenticated caller can substitute another order identifier in a request. Permission for the specific object must not be inferred from a valid identifier.

context.concept_name: Authentication and authorization tests including invalid-token rejection

coverage.learning_objective: Verify API authentication and authorization rejection: test one protected resource with invalid, insufficient and valid credentials.

required_facts.statement: Send requests through the real protected HTTP endpoint with absent, malformed and supplied bearer credentials, keeping the authentication and verification gates active.
Test invalid-signature, expired and contextually wrong tokens separately from a valid token, asserting credential rejection before protected output is returned.
Test an otherwise valid credential lacking the required permission separately from a valid sufficiently permitted credential to distinguish authentication from operation authorization.
Test a valid caller against another caller's object identifier as a separate deny path from missing operation permission.
Assert the declared status and safe body for each denial and the public projected result for the fully authorized request, not merely that some requests fail and one succeeds.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A protected order endpoint needs tests of distinct denial gates as well as full success. One rejected request does not prove every security boundary works.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Send requests through the real protected HTTP endpoint with absent, malformed and supplied bearer credentials, keeping the authentication and verification gates active.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Test invalid-signature, expired and contextually wrong tokens separately from a valid token, asserting credential rejection before protected output is returned. Test an otherwise valid credential lacking the required permission separately from a valid sufficiently permitted credential to distinguish authentication from operation authorization. Test a valid caller against another caller's object identifier as a separate deny path from missing operation permission. Assert the declared status and safe body for each denial and the public projected result for the fully authorized request, not merely that some requests fail and one succeeds.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Exercise the real endpoint with absent, malformed and supplied bearer credentials while keeping extraction and verification active. Separate invalid signature, expiry and wrong token context from a valid credential. Next use a valid credential lacking operation permission, then a valid caller requesting another caller's object. These isolate authentication, operation authorization and object authorization. Finally send a fully authorized request and assert the public projected result. For every denial, assert declared status and safe body before protected output is returned. Label each test by the gate it proves, not merely "fails." Substituting away verification would weaken the evidence precisely where this exercise requires real rejection behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: One denial plus one success is not complete security coverage. Isolate each credential and authorization failure while real gates remain active.
